A DDoS attack is rarely just “too many requests” — it’s a systems-design stress test that exposes where your architecture assumes normal traffic.

Under the hood, a resilient setup typically follows a defense-in-depth flow:

1) Edge triage (before your app exists)
- CDN/WAF drops malformed or known-bad patterns
- Geo/IP reputation + bot detection helps reject obvious fakes
- The goal: reduce attacker work without spending your backend budget

2) Rate limiting & request shaping
- Per-IP / per-route limits prevent “one noisy neighbor” from dominating
- Token bucket / leaky bucket semantics maintain predictable behavior

3) Admission control & backpressure
- When you’re at risk of collapse, refuse quickly (BUSY × REFUSED)
- Protect downstream dependencies via circuit breakers and bounded concurrency

4) Load absorption + graceful degradation
- Queue-based buffering absorbs short spikes
- Caches keep CPU steady (e.g., CALM · CPU 14%) by serving hot content
- In overload, switch to degraded responses so real users are still served (SERVE ✓)

Trade-offs to call out in production design + interviews:
- Edge filtering reduces backend load, but false positives can harm real traffic.
- Aggressive rate limiting improves stability, but can create user-visible throttling.
- Queues prevent immediate failure, but you must cap queue growth to avoid memory/latency death spirals.

If you’re preparing for “System Design & Software Architecture Explained” style questions: diagram the full path from the first SYN/HTTP request to the final response, including what happens during overload.
